`docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` names that as the strongest rung (R1, *unrepresentable*), C248's
`reject_whole_blocks` deletion is the worked precedent, and C252's close cell has the shape in one line
("the panic is unrepresentable rather than guarded"). So every open row was re-derived against today's
tree in three questions: **is the mechanism still representable**; if it is, **does the scenario still
reproduce**; and only then, what is the work.

It mattered because `dev` moved. Between the build **#315** was filed on (`b4f1cbfdb`) and today there are
**40 commits** — the self-reject carve-out (#316), the windowed catch-up, the fringe record store's
retirement with the claim travelling per block, and the walk's give-up — and rows filed in §73–§94 have
the same gap behind them.

**Eight rows close, and two of them close on a correction to their own text.**

- **C268 closed as unrepresentable *and* unreproduced.** Every exit of the page walk is checked and
  `node_syncing.rs` refuses an unfinished walk, so "a silent wedge in `NodeSyncing`" has no shape left;
  the history store is content-addressed and append-only, so no mechanism in the code can produce a
  non-advancing page; and the row's own record already says **three deliberate stagings, all healthy**.
  Its close cell also says why it can never have a theorem, which the row's own law knows: law 69's
  witness cell records that `ReachesTheGoal` is left unproved because the goal needs the **peer** to
  answer, and the peer is the adversary the model quantifies over.
- **C263 closed as superseded.** It waited on a tarball that lives only on the reporter's machine; the
  TE-1 witness has since landed **in this tree** and reads the four nodes together, and the question the
  row wanted ("which mechanism did the incident run") has been divided — the write loss is C216/C248
  (fixed, law 17c), the four heads are the witness's own subject. A close condition that names an input
  this programme cannot reach is discharged by the record.
- **C260's title was half wrong**, and the re-derivation found which half: no write is dropped (a
  final-scope chain is never applied *or* rejected; `rejected_finally` cascades only to a conflict-scope
  dependent). The reporting half was real and **wider than the row says** — such a rejection reached no
  surface at all, and I1's own filter exempts it by construction. The row survives, re-scoped, and the
  field that closes it is `MergeReport::final_scope_rejected_chains`.
- **C249 was a finding wrapped around a rung.** Its defect half is closed (both silent paths are loud,
  with counters on `/api/status`); the reset rung it also names is **F-U5-01 on the failure-HAZOP
  worksheet**, dispositioned R3, with its owed test and its ship-dark rule written down. This pass wrote
  "owned by #287" here, and **§98 corrects that**: the worksheet's own §5, C249's close cell and pass §73
  all say the per-node reset is a *separate unit* from the net-wide operator tool, so it was given an
  owner of its own (**#320**) rather than left attributed to an issue that is closing.
- **C254 landed its two residuals**: the source check `tools/check-spawn-observability.sh` (30 sites in
  eight ingress files — 6 supervised, 7 held, 17 bare-with-a-reason, both directions of staleness
  checked, negative control run) and the closed-channel count on the status surface.
- **C262's residue was a live hole**, not a hypothetical one: `rholang/src/system_processes.rs` reads
  `spec/conformance/protocol.tsv` from outside the formal gate's trigger list. The gate now checks its own
  trigger list, in both directions, from inside the gate — which needs no workflow edit to stay honest.
- **C255's last item** was one allowlist entry saying it covers a shape; **C256** closed on the decision
  its close condition allows, with the inert mechanism recorded in the deviation register (§6) and its
  three dead halves named as dead.

**What the re-derivation also showed, and it is a fact about the register.** **Six of the ten open rows
rested on a `candidate:` slug rather than a law** — C254, C255, C256, C262, C268, C269 — and a slug means
the property has **no theorem**, so "is this state still representable?" has no *formal* answer for those
rows. That is the same shape the OCapN wave was caught in ("an integration whose register rows are all
`candidate:` slugs has no laws"), and it is why a review driven by closure conditions could only tick
them. For C268 it is stronger still: no theorem *can* exist, for the reason its own law states.

**What stays open, and why that is not a failure of the pass.** **C259** and **C269** are the two rows
whose subject is genuinely a run: a net whose finality is frozen, a wiped joiner synced through an
operator-named anchor, and the tool naming that anchor. The state is still stageable — the divergence
instrument retired with the store it perturbed, and nothing had to replace it, because a sub-quorum net
freezes finality on its own (`up --validators 4 --fresh` reaches it unaided, `--no-autopropose` with
nothing deployed cannot move finality, and stopping validators below ⅔ freezes it on demand). **#315** is
decided by the same run, and #318 takes one of its two arms from it.

**The issues, re-derived too, and the criticism does *not* land there.** All seven open issues but #51
were filed in the last week, and the ones still open are open because they are *design decisions or
missing capabilities* — slashing by proof and a bounded denominator (#290), the reconciliation meet and
its live venue (#287), post-quantum signatures (#274), a process item (#51) — not because a defect was
filed against an older build. #315 is the single case where "reported against an older version" could
hold, which is why the rig tests it instead of assuming either way.

### §97's rig: the frozen net, the return, and the anchor (C259, C269, #315)

**One devnet session, four phases, and it settles more than the pass asked it to.** The rig is
`tools/devnet.sh up --validators 4 --fresh` — four bonded validators at 100 each, autopropose — and the
state worked for is a net whose **finality is frozen while the tip keeps moving**, which is what C259 and
C269 both wait on. It needs no instrument: **stopping two of the four leaves 200 of 400**, under the
strict two-thirds finality needs. (The divergence injection retired with the store it perturbed, and
nothing had to replace it — the state arises on its own.) Raw capture:
`spec/audit/evidence/n-anchor-drill/frozen-finality-recovery.txt`.

**The frozen state, measured.** Before the stops: h=68/69/67/67 with last-finalised 52 — a gap of 16.
Sixty seconds after `stop 2` and `stop 3`: the survivors at **h=125/125 with f=54**, so the tip moved
**57 heights while finality moved 2**, `autoproposeHalted=false` on both, and the gate's own reason:

```
finalityStall: a layer exists but its supporting stake is not a supermajority —
               200 of 400 (2 full partition(s) among 2 candidate(s))
```

That is `NoAdvance::Support` firing with the arithmetic this rig is built on — **the second arm #318
asked for**, and the first reading of that arm on a net where the freeze is *by construction* rather than
incidental.

**#315's question, answered on the current build: it resumes.** With the net frozen, `start 2` returned
the validator and finality moved **54 → 102**. #315's mechanism was that a returning validator "has not
*sent* a block since restarting", so the peers' latest-message views still held its pre-outage messages
and `quorum_reachable` stayed false — and that is not reproducible here. The stated prediction before the
run was that it would resume; it did. What that does **not** settle is the live incident's own history (a
partition, then a rebuild of the instance), which is a state this box cannot reach — so the issue gets the
result and the distinction rather than a close it has not earned.

**C259's owed clause, met: the walk completes on a net whose finality is frozen.** The trick is *which*
validator to wipe: **a survivor** — its stake is bonded whether or not its node is serving, so wiping
validator 1 keeps the net at 200 of 400 and frozen, while wiping a *stopped* one would return its stake
and unfreeze the net (which is #315's question, not this one). Validator 1, wiped and started with
`--sync-anchor <the anchor at height 52>`, logs its own path:

```
Syncing to the operator-named anchor a5655cd4… rather than to a fringe a peer offers: with finality
  frozen no peer has one, and the answer to an ordinary fringe request would be the genesis block
LFS state is successfully restored.
catch-up against devnet-bootstrap: this node's frontier is height 52, walking outward in windows of 8
```

— with the master at h=182, f=110, still reporting the `Support` stall. So the walk the row owed, on the
state it owed it on, completes.

**C269's owed run: the tool names the operator's block.** With all four nodes readable,
`RECONCILE_ANCHOR=<the same hash> tools/reconcile-network.sh` exits **0** and prints:

```
== 3. the anchor ==
  the operator's anchor: height 52, hash a5655cd4f219aca6c40247ddf61a6d868987d9f6c7572667aa6fd0712f5b929b
  This is **your** root, not a computed meet: this tool has verified that devnet-bootstrap holds the block
== 4. what is above the point ==
```

which is the row's close condition word for word: the anchor stated as the operator's choice rather than
a computed meet, the nodes' disagreement reported rather than resolved, and what is above the point
enumerated. **The honest limit, unchanged from the plan**: this net keeps a *usable* last-finalised
block, so the tool's computed-meet path would have accepted it too — what the run exercises is the
operator-named path, not the refusal it was built for.

**C268's close condition, met on demand — after a staging of the same rig looked stuck.** The
frozen-finality session ended with a plain `reset 3` against a producing master at h=265, and at t+45 s
the joiner had **385 requests and no restore, height 0** — which reads like the row's shape. It is not
evidence of it, and the reason is the row's own discriminator: that capture counted *requests* and not
*paths*. Re-running the same staging with the discriminator
(`spec/audit/evidence/n-anchor-drill/c268-fourth-staging.txt`) is unambiguous:

```
t+ 40s  requests=48   distinct-paths=48
t+ 60s  requests=172  distinct-paths=171
t+100s  requests=184  distinct-paths=171  restored=1  joiner h=86  master h=182
```

**171 distinct paths out of 172 requests**, the count inside the recorded healthy control's range
(153–226), and `LFS state is successfully restored` with the joiner climbing from 0 to 86. The cursor
advances through distinct paths and never repeats a slice — which is what "the page walk advances" means,
and it is the row's own close condition rather than an argument from absence. The phase-F count is
recorded in the capture as what it is: a walk still in progress when the window closed.

## 98. The meet, and the two artefacts it needed (C272, #287)

**What this pass is.** `#287` — the reconciliation utility — has held two things open since §89: the
**meet** and the **venue**. The venue is a live-testnet drill this box cannot run (no droplet key) and is
recorded as owed below. This pass is the other half: the user's ruling was to **build the meet properly**
rather than re-scope it away, and doing that turned out to require something the tree did not have.

### The two facts that decided the design, neither of which was in the issue

**1. There is no artefact by which a report can be attributed to a bonded validator.** The whole route
table (`node/src/web/http.rs`) has no `sign`, `nonce`, `challenge`, `identity` or `publicKey` endpoint,
and `ValidatorIdentity` (`casper/src/validator_identity.rs`) is never serialised. So obligations 1 and 2 —
"an endpoint bound to a bonded validator" and "a signed vote" — did not exist to be read.

**2. And the block API could not be self-verified either, which is the deeper one.** `LightBlockInfo`
carries `sender`, `sig`, `sigAlgorithm`, `justifications`, `bonds`, `blockNumber`, `seqNum` and
`postStateHash` — everything a meet needs — but `construct_light_block_info`
(`casper/src/api/block_api.rs`) maps a stored `BlockMessage` *into* it, and the canonical protobuf the
hash is taken over is not reconstructible from it: deploys lose their raw encoding and
`state.system_deploys` is dropped outright. A client could therefore prove *"key S signed the 32-byte
value H"* and could not prove *"H is the hash of the block whose height, seq_num, bonds and
justifications are these"*. Every field a recovery decision rested on was the node's word — which is
exactly why weighting reports would have been "another inferred quorum", the error class #302 already
paid for once (a proposer's stake summed once per *observation*, printing "400 of 400" for one
validator's 100 of 400).

**And one path was closed rather than taken.** The tool could have re-derived the finality rule client-side
— walk `justifications`, compute the supporting stake, decide "finalised". It must not: the codebase's own
note on `NoAdvance` (`block-storage/src/dag/finalizer.rs`) says two implementations of one rule can
disagree (`Split`, law 51b), and a recovery tool is the last place that should be discovering a second
implementation that disagrees with the first. So the split is deliberate: **the finality rule stays in the
node; only the two checks a client genuinely needs move out, and they move as the node's own functions.**

### What landed

**The node's artefacts (C272).** Two read-only additions, both in law 43's catalog:

- `GET /api/block/{hash}/raw` (`RawBlock`) answers with `to_bytes_cleared()` — *exactly* the preimage
  `hash_block` hashes — plus the signature over that hash. A client hashes the bytes, compares to the
  claimed hash, verifies `sig` under `sender`, and then reads the height, the seq_num, the justifications
  and the bond map off bytes it verified.
- `GET /api/finality-attestation?nonce=…` (`FinalityAttestation`) answers with the node's finalised block
  signed by its validator key over `blake2b256("rchain-finality-attestation-v1" || nonce || blockHash)`
  (`attestation_prehash`, one function shared by the signer and the verifier). The domain tag keeps a
  signature over 32 bytes from being reusable as another statement over 32 bytes; the caller's nonce is
  *signed*, so a reply captured from an earlier run is not an answer to a later one; and the signature is
  what makes a false finality claim attributable rather than anonymous.
- `rnode verify-block` / `rnode verify-attestation` are the verifiers, as subcommands rather than shell
  code, so the checks are `casper::proto_util::hash_block` and `casper::validate::block_signature` — the
  node's rules, called once.

**The meet (`tools/reconcile-network.sh` §3).** Every node attests; every block the tool touches is
verified; the anchor is the **deepest block a strict supermajority of stake has finalised**
(`3 * stake > 2 * total` on integers — exactly two thirds is not one). Nodes are ordered by the height
they attested and accumulated until the stake clears the threshold, so a lagging node neither drags the
point back nor vetoes the recovery; nodes *at* the crossing height are kept, because dropping them would
name a laggard that is not one; and the ones left out are printed. Where the subset's attested blocks are
not on one branch, the candidate is the shallowest and is walked down its own **verified** ancestry until
it is an ancestor of every member — bounded, and a refusal at the bound rather than a point guessed below
it.

**Obligation 4 stopped being decorative.** §2 has *reported* equivocation since #308 from the block API's
own `sender` field — one endpoint's word — and nothing consumed it; C261 called that out as the second of
its two guesses. §3 now **proves** what it can: two distinct blocks by one sender at one height, *each
fetched and verified*, with the sender taken from the verified bytes. A proven equivocator's stake leaves
the numerator **and** the denominator, which is the only way a pool may legitimately shrink, and never by
silence: a threshold that drops when a validator goes quiet would let whoever can silence honest nodes
finalise with a minority. The proof scans a bounded window of heights around the deepest attested block
and prints which, so the absence of a proof reads as a bound rather than a clean bill of health.

**Three refusals are new, and each is a shape the old gate could not see**: two endpoints attesting as one
validator (one bond is one weight — counting it twice is how a single stake passes the threshold), a node
attesting as a key the pool does not bond, and nodes whose verified bond maps differ (different
denominators are not arithmetic; they are the state divergence the design says to stop on).

### What the old gate was, and why it could not simply be repaired

Until this pass §3 required every node to report the **identical** finalised height and hash. That was
honest — it can only refuse, never fabricate — and unusable in the state the tool exists for. The
measurement is in the tree: on a four-validator net with two stopped, the three survivors read finalised
**102 / 97 / 110** (`spec/audit/evidence/n-anchor-drill/frozen-finality-recovery.txt`). That is an
ordinary producing chain, not a disagreement — unanimity is not a property a producing chain has — so the
gate refused precisely where recovery was needed, and the operator's only way through was to name the
anchor themselves (`RECONCILE_ANCHOR`), which is a **root the tool must not present as computed**. The
meet keeps that path for the state it is still needed in — a net with no finality left — and lifts the
refusal from the ordinary case.

### The record, corrected

- **C272** is the new row: *the block API answered with a summary a client cannot verify*, closed on the
  two routes and the verifier, with the class named as the reason C261's obligations existed.
- **C261's close cell** said the four obligations "stay on #287, which stays open as the meet's issue".
  They do not stay anywhere: the meet landed, which was C261's *first* alternative, after it closed on the
  second (the anchor gate stated as the design, which was right for the tool as it then was).
- **The runbook** (`docs/src/node/testnet.md`) said "a stake-weighted meet … issue #287's design, **which
  is not implemented here**". It is implemented now, and the page describes what the tool computes.
- **`docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` §5** still quoted #287's *superseded* design ("read
  `last-finalized-block` from every node and **stop if they disagree**") — the rule the issue corrected on
  2026-10-09 and this pass replaced. And **F-U5-01's owner cell** said `(owner: #287)` while §5 of the same
  page, C249 and §73 all say the per-node reset is a *separate unit* that is "not yet anyone's", and §97
  said "owned by #287". Adjudicated to §5: the per-node acting half is not #287's, and §287's close would
  otherwise leave an R3 rung unowned, so it gets an owner of its own.
- **`docs/src/spec/testnet-acceptance.md`** recorded "**Recovery from the divergent finality itself:
  none** … the only 'recovery' documented is the operator restarting onto a chain it never synced". That
  was true when it was written and is not any more: the utility exists, its operator path is exercised on
  a frozen net, and its meet is exercised on a devnet. The clause now cites those runs.

### What this pass does not close

**The venue stays owed.** The acceptance names a live-testnet drill; this box has no `~/.ssh/id_droplet`,
and the tool's non-local rows drive `curl`, `systemctl` and `tar` over SSH, so the apply half is not
runnable here. The live net also runs `b4f1cbfdb`, which has neither new route, so the *new* meet cannot be
exercised against it either until the live build moves. The read/plan half *is* runnable over plain HTTP
and is recorded as far as it goes — named as a bound rather than reworded into a pass.

**And the meet does not close C259.** Where nothing is finalised there is no block to meet *on*: the
store-level restore remains the mechanism for that state, and `--restore-from-master` remains a labelled
stopgap rather than a sync.

### §98's rig: the meet on four real validators

One devnet session (`tools/devnet.sh up --validators 4 --fresh`, autopropose, image rebuilt from this
branch), three arms. The transcripts are `spec/audit/evidence/n-reconcile-drill/meet-*.txt`.

**1. Lockstep — the meet computes.** `meet-lockstep.txt`. Every node attests, every attestation and every
block verifies, the four bond maps agree, the strict supermajority is 400 of 400, and the point is the
deepest block all four finalised (height 71). Exit 0 in plan mode. Two readings worth keeping: §1's
`/api/last-finalized-block` readings already differ (63/63/63/62) while the *attested* blocks agree — the
summary reading and the validated finalised block are not the same thing, which is part of why the meet
attests rather than reads — and the mean per-height block count above the point is 3.5 (four siblings per
height, one per validator), which is the DAG's normal shape and not a divergence.

**2. A lagging validator — the case the gate could never handle, and the reason this pass exists.**
`meet-lagging-validator.txt`. Validator 3 was stopped while the other three ran, then restarted while it was
still catching up. Immediately: §1 shows four *different* finalised readings (273 / 273 / 273 / 94), which
is the state the unanimous gate refuses by construction. The meet accepts — the three live validators
attest the same block at height 285, the returning one attests height 97, the fraction is **300 of 400 =
75 %**, the subset is the three, and V3 is printed as **"not in the subset (lagging, not vetoing)"**. That
is Jim's correction working as the issue states it, on a real net: the laggard neither drags the point back
to its own height nor vetoes the recovery, and it is rewound onto the master's DAG like any other joiner.

**3. A node that does not answer — silence stays silence.** `meet-node-down.txt`. With two validators
stopped, the two survivors attest the same block and the tool still refuses, because an unweighed node is
not an agreeing node: *"REFUSING: V2 did not answer the attestation request"*, with the way out named (the
node file, or `RECONCILE_ANCHOR`). Excluding a dead node is the operator's call and stays printed as theirs;
the tool does not infer it.

**And the live arms found two defects the offline fixture could not**, both now fixed and both recorded in
that commit: the verifier's verdict was being read through `rnode`'s **stderr** — which is not empty, since
jemalloc writes ~190 KB of allocator statistics there at exit (`stats_print:true`, `.cargo/config.toml`),
so merging the streams put the dump in the middle of the JSON the tool parses — and the equivocation scan
was looking **inside one endpoint**, where the evidence is not: a node refuses its peer's twin, so it holds
only one of the pair, and the scan must aggregate the endpoints and verify the two blocks it finds. The
first defect is the class F-U10-03 names (a diagnostic on the wrong surface); the second is a property of
the protocol that a stubbed fixture cannot show.

**The fourth arm — a live proven equivocation — was attempted four times and did not run, and the two
reasons are worth more than a green line would have been.** It is recorded here at the length it took,
because the next person to try it should start from where this got to rather than from the start.

*First obstacle — `reset` cannot arm a node cheaply.* The obvious way to add `--equivocation-injection` to a
running net is `tools/devnet.sh reset <n>`, which is the only path that recreates a container with new
flags — but `reset` also wipes that node's store, so the armed validator rejoins empty against a producing
master. It never caught up: 25 minutes in it was still in the LFS phase at height 0 while the master had run
to **678**, because the chain keeps growing while it hydrates (the "a joiner against a producing master"
shape C268 and C259 record, and the reason the windowed catch-up exists).

*Second obstacle — arming it at creation is not sufficient, because the armed validator must also be
**drawn**.* The injection was then armed on a node at `up` time — three attempts, once on a validator and
twice on whichever node the log showed proposing — and in every attempt the armed node turned out to be the
one the epoch's **active-set draw** left out. A validator outside the active set does not propose at all: its
own log says *"not proposing: … is not in the active set this node reads, which is the newest block's bond
cache — either it is not bonded, or the draw left it out for this epoch"*. No proposal, no twin, no
equivocation. `--active-validators 4` did **not** force the set (each of the three nets read
`active=3` of 4 bonded), so the staging that remains is to give the armed validator a dominant stake
(`--stakes`) so the stake-weighted draw picks it, or to pin the draw — a devnet-tooling question, not a tool
question.

*One useful observation fell out of the failed attempts.* The net routinely runs with **3 of 4** bonded
validators in the active set, and the meet still computed **400 of 400** in the lockstep arm: every bonded
validator attests, including ones that are not proposing, because attesting needs a *finalised block* and not
a turn at proposing. That is the property the meet's arithmetic assumes, and it now has a live witness
rather than an argument.

What *is* exercised for obligation 4 is the arithmetic: three fixture cases (a proven equivocator leaving
both sides of the fraction, the proof named with the pool it shrinks, and the equivocator's attestation not
being allowed to set the meet) plus the aggregation fix the live run forced — a scan that reads one endpoint
cannot see a pair a node refuses to hold.

## 99. The stall that was not a stall: an operator surface counting a producing chain's ordinary state (C273, #318)

**The finding, and it came from a rig built for something else.** On a four-validator autopropose devnet
where every validator was producing and every sampled height's block-hash set was identical across all four
nodes, `finalityStallEpisodes` read **136-152** after about 212 blocks — roughly one "episode" per round —
while last-finalised advanced throughout (195-198 against tips at 212-213). The chain was healthy; the
number said it was not. That measurement is `spec/audit/evidence/n-anchor-drill/divergence-fixed.txt`, and
#318 was opened because it fit no row.

**Why it happened, read off the gate rather than argued.** `note_finality_stall` counted a
not-stalled → stalled transition on every observation, and the stake gate refuses the derivation on *most*
blocks of a healthy round. A block justifies only the messages that existed when it was built, so what the
gate sees is a partial layer — one validator's candidate seen by the whole partition — and its own refusal
says so:

```
a layer exists but its supporting stake is not a supermajority — 100 of 400 (1 full partition(s) among 1 candidate(s))
```

That is the ordinary state between the first and the last block of a round. What the payload did *not* say
is how many senders the partition had, so **a healthy mid-round refusal and a stuck node rendered as the
same string**, and `finalityStall`'s description on the wire — "why finality is not advancing" — told an
operator to read it as an alarm. The two readings disagreed because the counter was measuring rounds, not
health: the number it reached was a function of how long the net had been running.

**The answer to #318's first question, then: yes, ~1 stall-entering per round was expected — because the
counter was counting the wrong thing.** The gate is not wrong to refuse a partial layer: the derivation
advances when the layer completes, which is what "finality advances once per round" means. So the fix is
the signal, not the gate, and #318's second question — the stable ~15-height lag — is untouched by it and
still owed its own measurement with a stated expectation.

**What landed.**

- **The gate's refusals carry the partition.** `NoAdvance::Coverage` and `NoAdvance::Support` gained
  `partition`, taken from `partition_bonds` at the refusal site — the gate's own arithmetic rather than a
  second copy of it (`Split`, law 51b). The reason string names it:
  `… 1 candidate(s) of a 4-sender partition`. That is #318's instrument, permanently: the reading is now
  self-describing rather than needing a rig that logs the layer beside it.
- **An episode is a sustained run.** The threshold is **`2 × partition` consecutive refusals**, which is
  not tuned: a healthy net advances the derivation at least once per round — that is what a round *is* —
  so the longest run of refusals a healthy net can show is bounded by the partition. Twice it is a run no
  healthy net reaches, and it **scales with the net**: eight refusals are a stall on four senders and
  pacing on thirty. The test pins both ends.
- **`finalityStalled` is on the surface.** The counter's own stated purpose was always "so 'stalled now' is
  distinguishable from 'stalled and recovered'", and it could not serve that purpose while a refusal was
  the ambient state of a producing chain. The reason string stays the per-observation *diagnosis* (F-U10-01
  asked for it on every observation, and that stands); the boolean is the state to alarm on.
- **The progress guard counts nothing.** `AlreadyPublished` — the derivation would publish what is already
  finalised — is neither a refusal nor an advance, so it no longer feeds the run: a quiet chain must not
  look stalled.
- **The descriptions say what the numbers are.** The DTO's doc comment, the OpenAPI property text and the
  `Envelope.lean` row all move with the new key (`finalityStalled`), so the served document a client
  generates types from no longer describes a diagnosis as an alarm.

**What is *not* claimed.** This does not make the surface a health verdict: `finalityStall` is still the
gate's verdict on the last block validated, and on a producing chain it is usually `Some(..)`. The
distinction the fix buys is between *pacing* and *stalling*, which is what an operator reads it for — not a
licence to treat a non-null reason as a fault.

**And the row this refines.** F-U10-01 exposed the surface and is right to have done so; what it could not
know is that the counter it exposed would count partial layers. Its cell now carries the refinement and
points here, and its stale falsifier citation (the test was renamed by this pass) is corrected to the
re-derived line numbers and the new test name.

## 100. The node resets itself: the third rung, and the residue reading found (C274, #320)

**The rung, and why it waited.** The disposition ladder's third rung — *detect a node that cannot heal,
say so, then reset to a known-safe state and catch up* — was recorded as **entirely unbuilt** for a running
node, and the page's own headline said so: the node does not mostly wedge silently, it *fails loudly and
then does nothing*. §82 built the dark half on purpose (the detector, `unrestorableRecords`, the dry run,
and the primitive `drop_above` with its denominator `rewind_plan`), so that when the acting half landed
there would be a real numerator to judge it against. This is that half.

**The shape, and the alternative that was rejected.** A reset could have re-entered `NodeSyncing` — the
boot-only machine. It should not: that machine is bulk LFS sync, its importer is *moved* into a spawned
task, and a rewound node is in exactly the shape `--sync-anchor` already handles — it holds a chain up to
a finalised anchor and needs everything above it. The catch-up walk does that, and it runs in the
**running** phase. So the reset is a rewind, a body purge, a runtime root reset and a walk restarted from
the anchor, and the node never leaves `NodeRunning`. The decision was made *before* any code, from the
engine's own structure, which is what kept the unit reviewable.

**The decision is pure and the arms are not merged.** `reset_decision` takes `rewind_plan`'s three shapes
and returns one of three answers; only the shape with an anchor **and** its height acts. The middle shape —
a finalised block the view cannot place, because the height map leaves out validation-failed blocks — had
been logged by the dry run with the *no-anchor* sentence, which is false of it, and `drop_above` takes a
*height*, so acting there would have handed it genesis. The two refusals are different facts and are now
different answers, which is the same separation the plan's two arms were introduced for. The fourth shape
the type system demands (`(None, Some)`) is folded in, named, and unreachable — `rewind_plan` derives the
height from the anchor.

**The residue, and this is the part worth carrying forward.** `drop_above` rewinds the DAG and leaves
`BlockStore` alone (it does not own it). A node that kept the bodies would keep *serving* blocks it can no
longer replay — and, worse, its receiver reads a body that is stored but absent from the DAG as **"stored
but not yet validated"** (`block_receiver::not_validated`), adds it to `parents_to_validate`, and
`send_to_validate` puts it back on the incoming queue. So the next child of a dropped block arriving would
**re-insert the dropped block above the anchor and undo the reset** — the node's own pipeline restoring
what the node deliberately discarded. The fix is not a guard: the reset deletes the bodies `drop_above`
returns, which is what those hashes were returned for, so the rewound state is **unrepresentable** — there
is nothing left to serve or to re-inject. R1, reached by reading rather than by a rig.

**What the rung still owes, named rather than implied.**

1. **The engine-level test.** No harness drives `apply` — only `node_runtime` calls it — so the running
   loop's third exit is pinned by reading, not by a run. The row's own owed falsifier (*a diverged running
   node re-enters sync*) needs an `apply`-level fixture, and the devnet arm is blocked: the divergence
   staging instrument retired, and an injected node's blocks are un-validatable by a clean node anyway.
   What *is* tested is the decision (four shapes, one unreachable) and the gate (off, on, refused-
   standalone).
2. **The persisted marker.** The rewind and the body purge are two store operations. A process that dies
   between them leaves bodies with no DAG entries, which the re-insertion arm reads as awaiting validation
   again — so the crash window needs the node to know, across a restart, that it is rewound.
3. **The Lean step — closed in the same unit, as law 53 clause c.** `Stranding.lean` now models the port's *second* inverse: `rewindStep` (a **prefix** drop, not the unmark `restoreStep` is — a rewind discards the state the refusal was about, it does not clear the refusal), `strandSystemRewinding`, and two theorems — `the_refusal_is_not_persistent_once_a_rule_rewinds` (the falsifier fired a second time) and `a_rewind_is_not_available_without_an_anchor`, which is the **guard** and the reason the step is stated over a state that carries the precondition rather than over the list alone. That last theorem is the one that could have been wrong: the port rewinds only where `rewind_plan` answers with an anchor *and* its height, and a model without the guard would have certified a relief the port withholds in two of its three states. **And the worksheet's falsifier was credited to the wrong fix**: it said R3 reddens `the_refusal_is_persistent`, and that reddening came from #125's restoring rule (clause b). F-U5-02's cell carries the correction. Three Rust witnesses ride with the clause — the decision's four shapes, the durable half, and the signal's contract — taking the gate's registry from 166 to **169, all passing**.

**And the switch.** `casper.self-reset`, **off by default**, refused at config load on a standalone node
(a rewind puts the node deliberately behind its peers and the blocks above the anchor are re-requested from
a peer, so a node with nobody to ask would trade a refusal for a truncated DAG). Not gated on `--dev-mode`:
that guard is for effects indistinguishable from a fault, and this one counts, logs and acts only on a
spent budget — a stranded production validator is exactly who needs it.

## 101. The reset's crash window, and the line the record draws across it (C274, F-U5-01, #328)

**What was owed.** §100 built the rung and named what it still owed, and the second item was the one with
a state attached: *"the rewind and the body purge are two store operations. A process that dies between
them leaves bodies with no DAG entries, which the re-insertion arm reads as awaiting validation again — so
the crash window needs the node to know, across a restart, that it is rewound."* The first item — an
`apply`-level test — is unchanged and is named again at the end of this pass rather than quietly dropped.

**Why the window is not a race to be narrowed.** The two operations are `dag.drop_above(height)` and
`block_store.delete(&dropped)`, and the second's input is the first's output — so the order is forced and
the reverse is worse. Bodies first would leave metadata whose bodies are gone: a node holding blocks it
cannot serve, refusing their children for want of a body it recorded as present. That is a wedge against an
oscillation, and the window cannot be closed by arranging two operations that have to happen in the order
they already happen in. What closes it is the node being able to **name** the state it is in when the
process stops.

**The record, and why it is two phases rather than a flag.** `ResetMarker { anchor, height, phase }`
(`block-storage/src/dag/dag_storage.rs`), persisted as 41 fixed bytes — anchor, height, one phase byte —
under one literal key in a dedicated store. `Rewinding` is written **before** the first destructive
operation; `Rewound` after the second returns. **The phase is load-bearing and that is the design's one
real decision**: a boot that finds `Rewinding` knows only that a rewind was *intended* and re-applies both
operations, but a boot that finds `Rewound` must re-apply **nothing** — by then the node may have caught up
and produced above the anchor, and a second `drop_above` would throw those blocks away. A boolean would
have made the second boot destructive on exactly the node that had recovered.

**Where it lives, and the three places it could not.** Not `block-metadata`: that store decodes *every* key
as a 32-byte `BlockHash` (`BlockMetadataStore::create`), so a literal key breaks the boot it is meant to
repair. Not the approved store, which `get_approved_block` reads and **nothing in production reads** — a
store with no reader is where the marker would go to be ignored, and its value ("the state this node
approved") is a different claim from "a reset this node performed and did not finish". So: a
`reset-marker` DB in the existing `dagstorage` environment, one key, following the `indexed-from` pattern
that already stores a height under a literal key. **And the reset refuses to run without it** — the
`BlockDagStorage::write_reset_marker` default *refuses*, as `update_metadata`'s does, because a reset whose
durable half cannot be recorded is one a crash can undo silently.

**The guard, and the half of it that is not the rewind's return value.** `engine::reset::resume_after_reset`
is the boot path's repair. On `Rewinding` it re-applies `drop_above` *and* purges by a **predicate** —
every body whose hash is absent from `dag_set` — rather than by what the rewind returned. That is the part
worth reading twice: after a crash *during* the delete, the rewind is already durable and returns `[]`, so a
purge keyed on its return value would delete nothing and the very bodies the receiver re-injects would
survive the repair that exists for them. The predicate is the same fact stated independently of the order.
It costs one enumeration of the block store, **paid only when a marker is present** — a rare, deliberate
state, not any ordinary boot — and it may take a legitimately in-flight body with it, which is harmless
because the node is entering catch-up on purpose and re-fetches what it needs.

**The marker is cleared by the walk, not by the guard.** `run_catchup` clears it when its **frontier is
above the anchor** — the condition is the walk's own result, not its exit reason. A walk that ended with
nothing above the anchor (a silent peer, a closed door) leaves the marker, so the next boot re-enters the
guard rather than reconnecting to a truncated DAG; clearing on mere completion would re-open exactly the
window the marker exists to close.

**What is tested, and what is read.** `casper/tests/reset.rs` gains two tests.
`a_crash_after_the_rewind_is_repaired_at_boot_by_the_marker` starts *inside* the window — it writes the
intent and runs the rewind through the same seam `rewind_and_purge` splits at, then asserts the guard
reaps the bodies the DAG no longer holds, keeps the anchor's own body, and **does not rewind again** on a
second call once the node has produced above the anchor (the one way this guard could do harm). Its premise
assertion is what makes the second call a real test rather than a no-op: the DAG is already at the anchor
before the guard runs, so the purge can only have come from the predicate.
`a_node_that_never_reset_is_not_touched_by_the_reset_guard` pins the other direction — no marker, no
repair, nothing purged — because a guard that passed its own test by changing every node's boot would be
the worse defect. Falsifier: the capability is absent on the pre-fix tree and the test does not build
there; what it pins is the store state a crash leaves and nothing else in the tree reads.

**What is still read rather than run, named.** (1) The call site: `node_launch::apply`'s `else` branch
calls the guard and, when it answers, hands the anchor to the catch-up walk below — the same five-lines-of-
wiring boundary §100 recorded for the arm, and the reason the guard is a function of its own. (2) The devnet
arm the row's falsifier asks for (*a diverged running node re-enters sync*). **It is stageable now** — the
natural four-heads divergence needs no instrument (`n-anchor-drill/self-reject-stall.txt`, `up --validators
4 --fresh`), where §100 recorded it blocked behind the retired injection — and it is unrun. Neither is
claimed as done here.
## 102. The merge's scope is parent-sensitive, and that is not a fork (F-U6-01, C248's residue 1, #328)

**What was owed.** F-U6-01's falsifier — *"two merges of one round under two scopes, comparing the merged
state at the already-finalised height"* — recorded as owed since C248 and named again as item 1 of #328,
where the claim is stronger than the row's: `round_parents` is re-snapshotted on every insert
(`block-storage/src/dag/message_state.rs::advance_round`), so two nodes holding one block set can hold
different round boundaries and *"two honest proposers at one height can merge different scope-sets and
reach different merged states. **This is a hard fork**"*.

**The measurement, on one block set in two arrival orders.** Five blocks — `g`, then `{a1 by A, b1 by B}`,
then `{a2 on a1, b2 on b1}` — with a non-empty bond map, because `advance_round`'s closing predicate is
vacuously true over an empty one and the construction would then measure nothing. The two orders differ in
one thing: whether `b1` or `a1` arrives first. The result, in
`casper/tests/merge_determinism.rs::an_arrival_order_moves_the_round_snapshot_and_not_the_scope_a_block_derives`:

- **the premise holds** — `dag_set`, `msg_map`, `child_map` and the height map are equal, so the two nodes
  really do hold one block set;
- **the snapshot differs, and by name** — one node's `round_parents` is `{a2, b1}`, the other's `{a2, b2}`.
  That is #328's first claim, measured;
- **the scope moves with it** — `MergeScope::from_dag` over the two snapshots returns two different
  conflict scopes, differing in exactly `b2`, the block only the second boundary has seen. That is #328's
  second claim, also measured;
- **and nothing forks** — for **every** block, the scope the production derivation builds from *that
  block's own justifications* is the same on both nodes.

**Why the fourth line is the answer.** A proposer's snapshot does not travel as a snapshot: it becomes the
block's `justifications`, and every node — the proposer included — derives that block's pre-state from
those justifications against its own DAG (`multi_parent_casper.rs::get_pre_state_for_parents` takes
`parent_hashes`, and every caller passes a block's, never its own round's). So the derivation is a function
of *(block, DAG)*, and two nodes with the same block set have the same DAG. Two proposers with two
snapshots produce two **sibling** blocks, each valid to everyone — ordinary multi-proposer concurrency,
which is what `validate.rs`'s `max(justifications) + 1 == block_number` rule exists to admit. The
"different parents, different pre-state" fact is real and is not a divergence: it is two blocks, not one
block with two states.

**What this refutes, and what it leaves.** It refutes the *fork* reading of #328's item 1, and #328's body
is corrected on the issue. It does **not** reach the other half of F-U6-01 — a boundary chain that carried
a deploy computing a different pot from its empty siblings at an epoch boundary — which is a question about
*which chains are in scope*, not about arrival order, and which needs an epoch-running fixture rather than
five blocks. C248's residue clause 1 keeps that half; what it loses is the part that read the scope's
sensitivity as a fork, which this pass measured and refused. The debt line moves with it
(`falsifiers owed: 14 → 13` — one from #330's F-U5-01 and one from here), checked by
`tools/check-hazop-worksheet.sh`.
## 103. C259 closes: the no-finality run exists, and the row was asking the wrong mechanism for it (C259, #328)

**What was owed.** One run: *"a net in the no-finality state converges to one head without a genesis"* —
a four-heads divergence with frozen finality, where **no node has a usable finalised block anywhere**. The
row has carried it since 2026-10-09, and §97 narrowed it to exactly this case ("what this row still owes is
the *no*-finality case … which the retired divergence instrument used to stage").

**The run exists, and it is the closed row's own acceptance.** `n-reconcile-drill/restore-disarmed.txt`,
third run: the meet is **genesis** (height 0 — which is what "no finalised block anywhere" *is*, computed
rather than asserted), heights 17/17/17/17, **identical per-height block hashes across all four nodes**
including the multi-block heights, the genesis block untouched, and **finality resumed to height 11 on one
hash** where every node had answered `"Finalized fringe is not available."`. That is all four of the
acceptance's clauses, and the row's own.

**Why the row had not closed on it, and the correction.** The row's own words: (b), the store-level
restore, *"is a stopgap and does not close this row"*, and (a), the anchor, *"is the unit that lets an
operator recover without a data-dir copy"*. Both statements are true and the inference drawn from them was
not: **(a) is structurally unavailable for the no-finality state.** An anchor is a block *above* genesis
that a supermajority agreed on; where nothing is finalised there is none, which is precisely the state.
Requiring the no-finality case to be closed by (a) was unsatisfiable by construction — and the state is not
uncovered, it is covered by (b), whose cost is a data-dir copy and whose semantics are an operator
asserting a winner (the tool prints the winner before applying it). So the row closes on **the run**, and
the division of labour is stated: (a) for the partial divergences (demonstrated: the frozen-net walk, and a
joiner anchored 300 heights below a tip reaching it in 98 s), (b) for the no-finality case (demonstrated
above).

**Two residues, re-homed rather than dropped.** The row named two besides the run, and both now live where
an operator meets them (`docs/src/node/testnet.md`): the **O(chain) tuple-space hydration** a restore pays
(316 state roots, ~2.5 minutes on the control) is a stated cost of the restore; and the **sidecar stores**
(`mergeable-channel-cache`, `native-changes-cache`) are not part of the state a sync transfers, so a
restored block regenerates them — named as an open decision (extend the sync, or bound the regeneration
once) rather than as a defect. A third named item is **moot**: `drop_above`'s "missing pruning of
`fringe_data_store`" cannot be missing, because that store retired with the per-block fringe claim (Law
66/68; C250's residue, C270). The only cache left to prune is `BLOCK_INDEX_CACHE`, and that is #328's item
2, where the rewind now prunes it with the bodies it drops.

**And the state is unstageable on purpose.** The instrument that staged it (C215's
`--merge-divergence-injection`) perturbed the retired `fringe-data` store *and* **reached block content** —
an injected proposer's `rejected_deploys` is computed under its own perturbation and written into the block,
so every block it published was un-validatable by a clean node. The flag survives as an inert,
self-disclosing tombstone (`casper/src/dag.rs`) rather than as a working instrument, and the natural rig
that now produces four heads (`up --validators 4 --fresh`, §92) freezes finality at a *usable* block
instead. That is a repair, not a gap.

**What is not claimed.** The chain in that run was produced under the retired perturbation, so its
**validity** is not what was demonstrated — its convergence and resumed finality are. And (b) is a stopgap
in the sense the row meant: it needs a data-dir copy and an operator's decision. Both are recorded on the
row and in the operator page rather than left implied.

## 104. The last unread clause of #315: the proposer's own `quorum_reachable`, after the mesh (—, #328 item 3)

**The clause, and why it had never been read.** #315's close condition had two parts. The first — *"the
chain resumes after a sub-quorum outage"* — was run and refuted on the current build (two of four stopped,
both restored, finality 54 → 102 with no operator action). The second was *"no `quorum_reachable=false`
persisting after the mesh is complete"*, and the runs that closed #315 captured the **API** surface:
finality advancing, every validator attesting. `quorum_reachable` is not on that surface at all — it is
computed in the proposer (`casper/src/blocks/proposer/proposer.rs`, `is_super_majority(live moving stake +
own stake, the whole bonded map)`) and rendered **only** into a log line, rate-limited to fire on change
and then every hundred tips. So the clause was a reading of a proposer-side line, and no run had read it.

**The reading.** Three validators, `--no-autopropose --propose-on-deploy`, deploys to drive production —
and deliberately **not** a fresh four-validator autopropose net, which self-diverges into the §92
self-reject stall and would have measured a different thing. Final heights 19/19/19, finalised 15. Of the
**16** collected `attestation at tip N: …` lines, **14 read `quorum_reachable=true`** and **2 read
`false`** — and both are the **genesis round**:

```
attestation at tip 0: withheld — … quorum_reachable=false … round=[04f700a4]
attestation at tip 1: licensed — … quorum_reachable=false … round=[04f700a4]
```

`round=[04f700a4]` is a **one-sender** round. The flag asks whether the live stake plus the node's own
reaches a supermajority **of the whole bonded map**, and on a round with one participant there is no
supermajority to reach — by construction, not by fault. That is the same reading `n213-results.md` recorded
for the first cut ("the round is its genesis alone, the exact state in which the first cut read
`quorum_reachable=false`"). From the moment the round is the full three-sender set
(`round=[04d8b6c3 04dbe32c 04f700a4]`) every line reads `true`, at tips 5, 6 and 18.

**So the clause holds, and the falses are named rather than excluded.** What this is *not*: a statement
about the N=8 shape, where the refusal is `400 of 800` **with all eight validators sending** — a stake
shortfall and not a one-sender round, and A1.3's own row; and *not* a general health check, because the
clause is about the flag not **persisting** false, and a chain genuinely short of a supermajority should
read false.

**Evidence.** `spec/audit/evidence/n328-quorum/` — `results.md` (the reading), `run.txt` (the raw capture),
`attestation-lines.txt` (the collected lines), driven by `n328-quorum-run.sh` in the same directory. One
host, one run.

## 105. A queued reset must reach the installed driver (C275, #338)

The request can exist before its waker. Installation previously recorded only the waker, leaving a pending request without a wake. The existing serial request test now fails on that ordering before the fix (CI run 38341642556, commit 0aff751). Installation takes the request lock before the waker lock, matching submission, and notifies the installed driver when the slot is occupied. Pending-driver handover and empty-slot installation are covered in the same test. This establishes local request delivery; it does not execute the full engine re-entry or prove global finalized-state safety.

Verified on 47540f5 by CI run 38342542544: the delivery regression, existing DAG/store reset tests, formatting/static gates and dependency checks pass. Casper reports 437 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored. C275 is closed for local delivery.

## 106. The durability rewinds: a HAZOP, and the laws it owed (C276–C278, #340's line)

PR #340 fixed one delivery bug in the self-reset and drew a line: *"full running-engine reset-to-sync
re-entry and universal finalized-state rollback safety remain separate acceptance boundaries"*. This pass
took that line as its subject — not as an audit-plus-fix, but as the repository's own method applied at
its own altitude: **HAZOP, root-cause analysis, and Lean4 first**. Every failure state is mathematically
representable, so a deviation is either *demonstrated* to be an instance of an existing law, or it earns a
**new law written before any Rust**.

**The HAZOP layer.** `docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` gained six study nodes, one per rewind site — U11
the reset request's lifecycle, U12 the durable rewind, U13 the runtime root, U14 the refusal budget, U15
the RSpace checkpoint, U16 the operator's reconciliation. Each dispositions all eleven IEC 61882 guide
words, carries Table A deviations with an RCA chain, and adds a **Table C — law coverage** naming the law
a deviation instantiates or the one it owes. Thirty-eight rows, twenty-three falsifiers owed, checked by
`tools/check-hazop-worksheet.sh --gate`.

**What an existing law already captured, and what it did not.** Law 53c's `rewindStep`
(`Rchain/Casper/Stranding.lean`) gives the rewind's *availability* (an anchored state) and its *effect* (a
refusal is removed) — but it is a pure state relation: it says nothing about durability, crashes, or a
completion record, which is the whole subject here. So four laws were written first, modelled on law 51's
`System`:

- **law 72** — a completion record brackets every durable effect (`Rchain/Durability.lean`);
- **law 73** — a raised request is not spent until the act commits (`Rchain/Requests.lean`);
- **law 74** — a checkpoint does not drain an overlay it has not folded (`Rchain/Checkpoint.lean`);
- **law 75** — a dependent action is taken only on a committed record (`Rchain/Attempts.lean`).

Each carries a **falsifier theorem that is red on the code as it stood** —
`an_early_commit_reaches_a_record_that_lies`, `a_split_take_reaches_a_state_that_spent_the_request`,
`a_drain_before_the_fold_reaches_a_state_that_lost_the_overlay`,
`a_raised_request_on_an_uncommitted_record_is_reachable` — and a non-vacuity witness. The register moved
from 71 laws / 95 entries to **75 / 99**.

**The Rust halves that landed** — law 72's and 73's with witnesses the formal gate runs, law 74's without
one, because its falsifier needs a fault-injection point the rspace tests do not yet have:

- the reset wrote `ResetMarker{Rewound}` when the two *stores* had returned and moved the runtime root
  *afterwards* — a durable `CURRENT_ROOT` write — so a crash between them left a record claiming the
  stores agree while the root named the dropped state, and the boot guard repaired nothing. The two
  marker writes now bracket all three effects, and the guard's `Rewinding` branch re-establishes the root
  (`casper/src/engine/reset.rs`, `casper/tests/reset.rs`);
- the reset request is spent only by the act that commits: the act peeks, runs the anchor pre-flight, and
  takes only once `perform_reset` has returned, so a failure that destroyed nothing leaves the request
  pending;
- `create_checkpoint` snapshots the native overlay before the drain and restores it if the fold fails, and
  records `last_native_*` only after the fold has committed (`rspace/src/rspace.rs`).

**What this pass does not claim.** The Rust halves of law 75, of F-U11-02 (the reset cells are
process-global while the reset state is per-shard), of F-U13's own crash-window falsifier, of F-U15-02/03
(the soft checkpoint's absent root; the leaf-before-root commit) and of F-U16 (the reconciliation tool's
missing journal, its same-minute aside collision, and its in-place systemd restore) are **owed**, each
named with its law or its `candidate:` slug in the HAZOP's Table C. The devnet arm that would exercise a
real reset end to end — stageable since §92 — is unrun.

**A correction this pass made to its own work.** The first draft carried a row (U11-02) claiming a
duplicate request strands a pending one. Reading `request_reset` against tokio's `Notify` shows the
opposite: `notify_one` stores a permit when no driver is waiting, so the first request's wake is not lost.
The row was wrong, the word is folded, and the debt adjusted — recorded here because a worksheet's
citations are claims, and this repository's rule is that a claim found false is corrected rather than
quietly dropped.

**Evidence.** `docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` (nodes U11–U16 and the debt line);
`spec/Rchain/{Durability,Requests,Checkpoint,Attempts}.lean` with register rows 72–75;
`casper/src/engine/reset.rs`, `casper/tests/reset.rs`, `rspace/src/rspace.rs`;
`tools/check-hazop-worksheet.sh --gate` and `tools/check-lean-conformance.sh` (173 Rust witnesses ran).

## 107. The durability rewinds, part 2: the stop, the shard, and the tool (C279–C283, #342's residue)

§106 landed the HAZOP layer, four laws and three of the Rust halves, and named what it did not reach.
This is that residue, closed in the same order — **a law written before the Rust** wherever the deviation
earns one.

**A law for the stop — 76.** §106's D3 was the sharpest thing it left: the reset's failed act says a node
in that shape "must not keep serving", and the LFS sync terminal says "this node is stopping rather than
serving a chain it never synced" — and **neither stopped anything**. Both are a `return Err` from a task
nobody joins; the launched `node_launch` future's error was only logged, and `NodeProgram::serve` never
awaited it, so the block receiver, the processor, the proposer and the API kept running. **Law 76
(`Rchain/Stop.lean`)** states the requirement — a reported fault and the stop are *one step*, and it is
the last step available — with its falsifier, `a_note_without_a_stop_leaves_the_node_serving`, exhibiting
exactly the port's old state: the latch set, the listeners up. The register is now **76 laws / 100
entries**.

**The Rust halves.** Four, and law 76's is the one with a witness the gate runs:

- **F-U12-03, the concluded stop (C279).** `shutdown::report_fatal` sets a latch the spawn wrapper writes
  and `main`'s wait selects on — a third arm beside the listeners and the signal — so a failed reset, and
  the terminal path that shares the sentence, **stop the process without draining**. No drain, because the
  fault means a store has moved under a view that was not rebuilt, which is the state the reset's own
  comment forbids serving from. Witnessed by
  `node/src/runtime/shutdown.rs::a_reported_fatal_resolves_the_wait_with_the_first_reason`.
- **F-U11-02, the reset cells are process-global (C280).** Both are keyed by the shard's lane
  (`ShardId::to_string()`): a node may be a member of several shards, each with its own DAG, block store
  and runtime, and the key is what makes "shard B takes shard A's request" **unrepresentable** rather than
  refused. That ordering mattered: with F-U12-03 landed, a misdelivered request refused at the anchor
  check would have killed the whole node. Keying over a config gate because the doctrine is to make the
  bad state unrepresentable rather than to guard against it.
- **F-U14-02, the request on the uncommitted record (C281).** `note_unrestorable_if_exhausted` now runs
  *after* the `update_metadata` that persists the count, in both paths, so a request raised by it names a
  count the store holds (law 75).
- **F-U16-01/02, the reconciliation tool (C282, C283).** The aside names are to the second and the docker
  branch **refuses an existing target**, where a same-minute retry used to re-tar the already-cleared
  volume over the only good backup; and the systemd `--restore-from-master` branch now stages beside the
  data dir and swaps each environment only once the whole copy has arrived, so the `"$n is unchanged"`
  it prints is true when printed.

**What this pass does not claim.** The tool's rows carry `candidate:` slugs, not laws — the tool is not
modelled, and a shell refusal is not a theorem; the two rows whose falsifier is a fault-injection point
the tree does not have (law 74's fold, law 75's write) stay **owed** in the HAZOP's debt line rather
than claimed. **F-U16-01/02 are no longer owed** (2026-10-30): their refusals are driven by
`tests/reconcile-docker-lifecycle.sh::test_backup_collision_is_refused` and
`tests/reconcile-systemd-restore-regression.sh::test_mid_stream_failure_leaves_joiner_unchanged`. F-U11-02's law is owed too — law 73's model is a one-shot
cell with one lane, and stating it per shard is a change to that model, not a citation. And the devnet arm
that would exercise a real reset end to end remains **unrun**.

**Evidence.** `docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` (F-U11-02, F-U12-03, F-U14-02, F-U16-01/02, and the debt
line at 22); `spec/Rchain/Stop.lean` with register row 76; `node/src/runtime/shutdown.rs`,
`node/src/main.rs`, `node/src/runtime/node_runtime.rs`, `casper/src/interpreter_util.rs`,
`casper/src/engine/reset.rs`, `casper/src/engine/node_launch.rs`,
`casper/src/multi_parent_casper.rs`, `tools/reconcile-network.sh`;
`tools/check-hazop-worksheet.sh --gate`, `tools/check-lean-conformance.sh` and the casper test suite.

## 108. The reset arm, attempted: the staging route §101 named no longer reproduces (C284)

§106 and §107 both left the **devnet arm** owed — F-U5-01's falsifier, *a diverged running node re-enters
sync*, the acceptance-level instrument for the self-reset — and §101 had recorded it as **stageable but
unrun**: *"now stageable with `up --validators 4 --fresh` (the §92 self-reject divergence needs no
instrument)"*.

**What ran.** `tools/devnet.sh build` (image at `731ac4b1c`, this tree), `down -v`, then
`DEVNET_EXTRA_FLAGS_devnet_validator_{1,2,3}="--self-reset" tools/devnet.sh up --validators 4 --fresh` — the
bootstrap plus three, which is the four bonded nodes §92's capture had, with the flag **confirmed present on
each container** (`docker inspect … .Config.Cmd`). Sampled every 15 s for ~9 minutes.

**What happened.** Nothing. Heights ran 98→270 (bootstrap), 149→277, 148→275, 144→271, and across the whole
run every node recorded **zero** `[fringe-divergence]`, zero `Self-created block …` and zero reset lines,
with `consecutiveSelfValidationFailures` 0, `autoproposeTimerHalted` false and `unrestorableRecords` 0
throughout. The net produced ~170 blocks and stayed healthy.

**Why, and this is the finding.** §92's self-reject came from the fringe-record store's **`min` tie-break**
on one key: two honest blocks finalising one fringe from two bases wrote the key, the `min` chose a
`state_hash`, and the node then refused its own block against the state that implied. That store is gone —
law 66/67/68's record redesign retired `join_fringe_records`, its `min` and the in-memory map
(`casper/src/dag.rs:812`, `models/src/block_metadata.rs:464`, `block-storage/src/test_support.rs:65`) — and
the `[fringe-divergence]` string that survives is a **reader-side** report of distinct claims, not a store
write. So §101's "stageable now" was true when written and is **false on this tree**: the divergence the
route relied on was fixed, and the arm needs a **new instrument** rather than a longer run.

**What this does not claim.** The reset's durable half, its boot guard and its ordering are pinned by
`casper/tests/reset.rs` and run by the formal gate (§106, §107) — this run says nothing about those. It says
the **acceptance-level** property F-U5-01 names is still **unrun**, and that the tree no longer has a
recorded way to stage it. That is the residue, stated rather than implied.

**Evidence.** `spec/audit/evidence/reset-arm/run.md` (the reading) and `observe.log` (the sampler's output,
136 lines). One host, one run; the devnet was torn down with `down -v` after the capture. The instrument the
arm now needs is designed beside them (`instrument-design.md`): a synthetic spent record written into a
stopped node's `block-metadata`, which reaches the drive loop's third exit — the half no test can — while
being explicit that it exercises the re-entry and not the healing. **That recommendation was refuted by
reading before anything was built — §109.**

## 109. The instrument design, refuted before it was built (C285)

§108's design recommended a synthetic spent record and pointed at it as what the arm needs. Reading the
code it was designed against refutes it, and refutes the obvious config route beside it.

**The synthetic record cannot reach the reset.** `restore_divergent_justifications` does not trust the
record: it re-runs `validate_checks` on the block (`casper/src/multi_parent_casper.rs:1178`) and
`revalidated_record` answers `Restored` for a block that passes — so a merely-*marked* valid block is
**cleared**, not escalated, and `restore_budget_is_spent` is only ever reached *through* a genuine
revalidation. Marking a spent budget from the start skips the restore path entirely, because
`restore_is_warranted` requires attempts left.

**And `--min-phlo-price`** — the devnet's own documented example for `DEVNET_EXTRA_FLAGS_*` — refuses with
`BlockStatus::ContainsLowCostDeploy`, whose cause is `FailureCause::Attributable` and **not** `Divergence`
(`casper/src/block_status.rs:132-160`): no restore, no budget, no reset. (That the status reads a *node*
input while being classified Attributable is the C198 nuance, not a route.)

**What survives.** `Divergence` is exactly five statuses, all of them — the map's own words — "decided by
this node's state or replay". So the instrument must make the node compute differently, which means a
different **code** or a different **trie**, and a trie edit that changes the computation breaks the node's
own reads first. The route is a **perturbed image**, with one constraint the genesis imposes: the
difference must be **outside the genesis path**, or block #0 fails and the node sits in `NodeSyncing`,
where the drive loop — and so the reset — does not exist. The **merge** satisfies it (genesis has no
justifications); the perturbed node would validate genesis, enter the running phase, and fail the first
merged block with `InvalidPreStateHash`.

**What this changes.** The route is known and constrained, and the arm is still **unrun**, so F-U5-01 stays
owed. What is *closed* is the wrong route, before it cost a build — this repository's rule is that a claim
found false is corrected rather than quietly dropped, and §108 published one.

**Evidence.** `spec/audit/evidence/reset-arm/instrument-design.md`'s correction, with its anchors;
`casper/src/multi_parent_casper.rs` (the restore's revalidation), `casper/src/block_status.rs` (the cause
map); `observe.log` beside it for the run the design was for.

## 110. The reset arm, attempted twice more: a partition and a state tamper (C286)

§108 tried the route §101 named and found it retired; §109 refuted the first replacement by reading. This
pass *measured* the next two, as the new plan's Phase 1 requires — each experiment cheap enough to kill its
own instrument, with the result written down either way.

**A partition stages nothing.** `up --validators 4 --fresh`, `docker network disconnect` on one validator
for 60 s: the two heads formed exactly as predicted (isolated node 98 and still producing; survivors
144/142) — and on reconnect it simply **caught up** (98 → 148), with the falsifier's grep returning **0** for
`state-hash disagreement`, for each of the five statuses, and for every link of the reset's chain, and
`unrestorableRecords` 0 throughout. That is `casper/tests/merge_determinism.rs`'s property — the merge is a
pure function of the parent set — measured live, and it agrees with the repo's own `n223-rejoin-results.md`
R3 (*"nothing is refused"*). `e1-partition.md`.

**A state tamper is effective and cannot be aimed.** The route the two refutations leave: edit the **state
the merge computes its base from**. A dev-only helper (`node/examples/tamper-fringe-claim.rs`) rewrites, on
a stopped node's volume, the greatest-height block's `post_state_hash` and its per-block
`fringe_state_hash` — both fields, because which one is read depends on whether a fringe exists
(`multi_parent_casper.rs:302` vs `:334-338`, and a fresh net is in the second). Six runs:

- tampering one node's own newest block: **nothing** — and the run *diagnosed* it, because the printed true
  claim was the empty state hash, which names the branch the merge actually takes;
- tampering **every** node's greatest-height blocks: **the chain stalls**, every node logging
  `propose failed … active-bonds leaf not found in state` — **the merge's own comment names that exact
  stall as the consequence of a wrong base** (`:248-252`). So the tamper *reaches the computation*;
- tampering one validator, then the three armed validators with the bootstrap left clean so it would keep
  publishing: **both absorbed**, heights advancing, zero markers.

**The conclusion, and it is about the trigger rather than about the drill.** The tamper works and the
mechanism is sound; the **aim** cannot be held. The trigger needs the tampered block to be the greatest
`(height, hash)` **justification of a block the subject validates** — and on a live net the target moves
every block, while a freeze-and-restart cannot pin it: the snapshot's max is already below the net's, and a
node re-fetching the block overwrites the tampered body with the true one.

**So the reset's trigger is not reachable by an external instrument at all — and that is by design.** A
`Divergence` must be *intrinsic*: the node's own state or replay against a block everyone else accepts. Any
difference applied from outside is either overwritten by the re-sync or is not the block the merge selects.
The narrowness is the feature — a trigger loose enough for an external edit would also fire on a healthy
node, and the reset is destructive. It follows that the arm can be staged only by an **intrinsic**
divergence, the perturbed *build* (the route §109/#345 recorded), and that route **exercises the drive
loop's third exit without satisfying F-U5-01's falsifier**, because a code-diverged node rewinds and fails
again rather than healing.

**What this changes.** F-U5-01's cell now says the arm is unrun *and why it cannot be run this way*, with
both attempts measured rather than asserted. The instrument is committed beside them
(`tools/reset-drill.sh`) with a header that states its own status, so the next reader does not rebuild a
route that has already been shown not to hold.

**Evidence.** `spec/audit/evidence/reset-arm/e1-partition.md` and `e2-tamper.md` (the readings, with the
numbers); `tools/reset-drill.sh` and `node/examples/tamper-fringe-claim.rs` (the instrument);
`casper/tests/merge_determinism.rs` (the property E1 measured live);
`casper/src/multi_parent_casper.rs:248-252` (the stall the all-node tamper produced) and `:302`/`:334-338`
(the two branches the tamper had to cover).

## 111. The standing reset marker, on the status surface (C287, F-U12-02)

§106's HAZOP left one deviation with the ladder's R2 shape and nothing to show for it: **the reset
marker's lifetime is unbounded.** `clear_reset_marker` has exactly one caller — the catch-up walk, and
only when its frontier passes the anchor (`casper/src/engine/catchup.rs:276-296`) — so a node that resets
and *cannot catch up* stays under a marker for ever, re-entering the boot guard at every restart, with the
residue reported only in a boot-time log line. Nothing a probe could ask said a marker was standing at all.

**The surface.** `GET /api/v1/status` gains **`resetMarker`** — null when the node is not mid-reset, else
the record rendered with its **phase**, anchor and height. The phase is the part that matters: `Rewinding`
is the state a boot repairs, `Rewound` is the state a boot only names, and an operator reading a stalled
node needs to tell them apart. The rendered height is the age proxy the row asked for: **a marker that
stands while `latestBlockNumber` does not move** is a repair that is not converging, which is readable
without watching.

**Where it is written, and why there.** The cell lives with the reset's other cells in
`interpreter_util` (`note_reset_marker` / `reset_marker_state`), and it is written by the **marker store's
own three methods** (`BlockDagKeyValueStorage::write_reset_marker`, `read_reset_marker`,
`clear_reset_marker`, `casper/src/dag.rs`) rather than at the call sites. That is deliberate: every writer
goes through those methods, so a future one cannot miss the surface, and the surface cannot drift from the
store it reports — the same reason `drop_above`'s trait forward exists two methods up.

**The envelope discipline moves with it, which is the part that is easy to forget.** A new status field is
`nullable`-and-**always present**, and law 43's catalog checks a *key set* — so
`spec/Rchain/Envelope.lean`'s `ApiStatus` row gained `resetMarker`, the corpus was re-emitted
(`spec/conformance/envelope.tsv`), and `node/tests/lean_envelope_corpus.rs`'s fixture gained the field. The
corpus test is the gate that holds the DTO's own serialization, the served OpenAPI schema and the Lean
catalog to one shape; it passed on the first run after all four moved together, which is what it is for.

**What this does not change.** The marker's lifetime is still unbounded — the row asked for a surface *or*
a bound, and the surface is the honest half: a bound would have to guess at how long a legitimate repair
may take, and the catch-up frontier is the only condition that knows. What changed is that a standing
marker is now **observable**, so "this node has been repairing for an hour" is a reading rather than an
inference from a log line nobody is watching.

**Evidence.** `casper/src/interpreter_util.rs` (the cell, and
`the_reset_marker_surface_follows_the_store`) · `casper/src/dag.rs` (the three writers) ·
`node/src/api/dto.rs`, `node/src/api/conversion.rs`, `node/src/api/web_api_impl.rs`, `node/src/web/http.rs`
(the field, the mapping, the schema) · `spec/Rchain/Envelope.lean` + `spec/conformance/envelope.tsv` +
`node/tests/lean_envelope_corpus.rs` (the catalog and its consumers) ·
`docs/src/spec/failure-hazop.md` F-U12-02.

## 112. The R3 rung closes over: each residue item's true state (—, F-U5-01)

The plan that took PR #340's line ("full running-engine reset-to-sync re-entry") listed five residue items
beside the arm. This pass **checked each one's true state rather than assuming it was owed** — and three of
the five were already where the plan asked them to be, which is worth recording because a residue left
unread is a residue somebody re-opens.

1. **F-U5-02's inverse — already dispositioned, not owed.** The row is R3 with `the_refusal_is_persistent`
   as its falsifier, and the theorem that answers it is law 53c's
   `the_refusal_is_not_persistent_once_a_rule_rewinds`; §101's correction already records that the
   reddening came from #125's restoring rule rather than from the rewind, and that the reset is a **prefix**
   step rather than an unmark. Nothing to add.
2. **F-U11-02's per-shard law — R1, and no theorem is owed.** The lane *is* the key
   (`ShardId::to_string()`), so "a request raised for shard A is taken by shard B" has no state to write: a
   per-lane model would make the bad state **unrepresentable**, and a law about an unwritable state
   restates its own definition — the register's `vacuous` status, which exists to stop exactly that.
   U11's Table C now says so, where it previously said "owed: the same request law, stated per shard".
3. **F-U12-02's marker lifetime — closed.** §111 / C287: the standing marker is on the status surface, and
   the HAZOP row carries the surface as its falsifier. The lifetime is still unbounded, and the row says
   why that is the honest half.
4. **The four owed falsifiers — each carries its seam decision *and its reason*, where the plan asked for
   the reason rather than silence.** F-U14-02: the `update_metadata` failure path has no injection point.
   F-U15-01: the fold's failure path needs a failing history store, which the rspace test modules hold
   privately (a new double for one branch; the *mechanism* it guards is already pinned at
   `rspace/src/native_store.rs`). F-U16-01 and F-U16-02: the tool has no test harness, so the refusal and
   the swap are pinned by reading. All four were recorded when their fixes landed; this pass confirmed the
   cells say so.
5. **TE-6, the net-wide rung — exercised, and now named.** The reconciliation's two halves are already
   measured: the **meet** over artefacts (§98, three arms including the lagging-validator and node-down
   refusals) and the **store-level restore that converged a stalled net** (§103,
   `n-reconcile-drill/restore-disarmed.txt`: heights 17/17/17/17 with identical per-height hashes and
   finality resumed to 11 where every node had answered *"Finalized fringe is not available."*). What was
   missing was the *name*: TE-6 appeared six times in the failure page and nowhere in the pass record, so

**What the rung still leaves, and it is one thing.** F-U5-01's own arm — *a diverged running node re-enters
sync* — is **unrun**, for the reason §110 measured: no external instrument can stage the trigger, because a
